paragraphs.text: The main policy story is at the FDA. The White House pulled Heidi Overton's nomination to be commissioner just hours before the Senate health committee was due to vote, according to STAT, Endpoints and Fierce. Reports point to uncertain Senate support: the NYT cites concerns over her stance on abortion and vaccines, and STAT describes a clash between GOP and MAHA figures over her record on vapes. The agency now has no nominee, which adds uncertainty for sponsors with pending reviews. Elsewhere in Washington, John Powers III was named permanent head of NIAID after a long vacancy. CMS proposed a sweeping Medicare integrity rule, branded CRUSH, that it says would save $90 billion across Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP and the exchanges. HHS also updated the HIPAA privacy rule to make it easier for patients to share records with apps. CMS says the Medicare Shared Savings Program saved a record $2.5 billion last year.

paragraphs.text: On public health, an international body has stripped the U.S. of the measles-elimination status it held since 2000, after falling vaccination rates let the virus regain a foothold. The WSJ quotes doctors and epidemiologists saying it could take five years or longer to regain, since that requires ending local transmission and keeping up surveillance. The loss was widely expected, but it is a visible marker of public-health erosion.

paragraphs.text: Approvals were busy. GSK won accelerated FDA approval for Nelkarmi (neladalkib) in lung cancer. It is the second drug from the $10.6 billion Nuvalent acquisition, and Fierce counts it as GSK's third high-profile approval in recent weeks, which helps validate that deal. Roche's breast cancer pill Wilserdly was cleared, and the company has said it could become its top seller. Novartis added an 11th indication for Cosentyx as it tries to cushion a 2029 patent cliff. Beren won approval for Lembaz in infantile-onset Niemann-Pick type C. In devices, MiniMed's tubeless Fit pump was cleared, and Medtronic is paying $380 million-plus for Contego Medical to build out its cardiovascular portfolio.

paragraphs.text: The setbacks were just as notable. The FDA's rejection letter for Summit and Akeso's ivonescimab goes beyond the overall-survival miss. It flags a possible VEGF-related safety concern and leans on China-heavy data. Endpoints says that raises questions about the wider class of PD-1xVEGF bispecifics, though the full picture is not clear from the excerpts. Merck ended three phase 3 blood cancer trials of nemtabrutinib after one study suggested the risks might outweigh the benefit. That closes out the program behind its $2.7 billion ArQule purchase in 2019. Alzheimer's had a mixed day. Priavoid's pill and Cognito's light-and-sound device both missed their trials. Biogen's tau-targeting diranersen showed a growing benefit at nearly two years. Sellas claims a phase 3 win in AML, which is company-reported only.

paragraphs.text: Private capital still flows to AI-driven biotech. Isomorphic Labs raised a record $5 billion Series C, co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia. That is the largest private raise in biotech history, six months after a $2.1 billion round, and it comes with no drug yet in the clinic. Marrow launched with $173 million to challenge gene therapy in sickle cell and beta thalassemia. Flagship is committing £100 million to a UK platform-company outpost. Onward raised a $28 million Series B. Vertex extended its discovery pact with Genomics for up to $220 million. The NYT reports that U.S. biotechs are sharing less with outsiders for fear that Chinese rivals will grab their ideas. That is relevant for licensing flows.

paragraphs.text: Nvidia dominates. Futures pointed higher after the chipmaker raised its forecast and its new chief said it was business as usual, following a sell-off triggered by revelations about Jensen Huang's personal affairs. The stock was up over 3% premarket, per MarketWatch, though JPMorgan warns of more near-term volatility. The board said it does not intend to reinstate Huang, and the NYT reports that Trump had urged him to fight for the job. MarketWatch notes Nvidia skipped its usual 10-Q filing, its first official signal that the resignation is about personal conduct. The WSJ says the results do little to settle longer-term questions. Scrutiny of dealmaking tempers the Street's optimism. Democrats are probing whether Commerce Secretary Lutnick helped Cantor avoid Nvidia losses, and the administration says it is investigating Megaspeed over alleged chip smuggling. European chip shares rose in sympathy.

paragraphs.text: The wider tape is shakier. The S&P 500 lost ground for a fourth straight session on Tuesday and closed at its lowest since late July. Bespoke notes it has also broken its 200-day moving average, though it argues the usual bearish read may not apply. Truist strategists say tech's 42% valuation reset invites investors to ask what could go right. The FT reports analysts expect global earnings growth to roughly halve next year, to 16% from 33.5%, as AI capex growth slows. Tencent's profit was flat as capex jumped more than sixfold. Corporate earnings show shoppers still spending: Lowe's raised its outlook, Target posted its strongest sales growth in about five years, and Walmart is benefiting from thrifty consumers. Analysts say Target still has to fix shoes and women's clothing.

paragraphs.text: Rates are the main pressure point. St. Louis Fed President Musalem said several hikes are likely needed before spring 2027. Gold fell 2.5% to its lowest in over a year on a firmer dollar and hike bets. One trader argues renewed bond weakness is a buying opportunity, while CNBC flags a tricky backdrop for bond investors. The Fed's own governance is also unsettled: Lisa Cook's lawyers say she will not attend the White House hearing on firing her unless a senior economic adviser is removed from the panel. The Bipartisan Policy Center estimates the U.S. could hit its debt limit by February.

paragraphs.text: Overseas, UK inflation rose to a one-year high of 3.6% in October, which the FT and WSJ link largely to energy costs. That keeps pressure on the Bank of England to raise rates further. MUFG argues that modest hikes could support sterling and growth. The FT says the household energy price cap is set to exceed £2,000 in January. The WSJ says supply-chain disruption from the Middle East conflict should keep inflation high well into next year even if a deal ends the U.S.-Iran war. Indonesia raised rates for the fourth time this year to defend a record-low rupiah. German investor confidence reached its highest since the war began. Oil fell on surplus expectations and bearish U.S. inventory data despite tanker attacks, and the FT says Russian petrol imports hit a record as Ukraine strikes refineries.

paragraphs.text: The tone at Bloomberg's Global Credit Forum in London was cautious. Davidson Kempner's Chris Krishanthan said a 'real fear factor' has developed. Bloomberg's summary says a sharp repricing across fixed income in recent months is likely to continue while rates stay elevated, shaking out weaker borrowers across industries. A kalkine piece notes high-yield spreads widened 11 basis points in a single session. That is a small data point, but consistent with the nervous tone. Apollo's Diego De Giorgi is positioning accordingly, focusing on investment grade and the short end of the curve, and expects a higher-rate environment.

paragraphs.text: The AI financing boom is drawing scrutiny. The ECB sees 'historic parallels' with the subprime bubble, citing concern that hyperscalers are building trillions of dollars of off-balance-sheet commitments through contracts with other tech groups. FT Alphaville separately calls next year's AI build-out financing 'increasingly funky' and questions whether the Nvidia backstop still adds up. Apollo's Europe head sees huge financing demand from AI, defense and power but says Europe's capital markets have not kept pace. That is a potential opening for private lenders.

paragraphs.text: Private credit keeps raising and deploying. BlackRock's HPS is seeking billions for a new direct lending fund. Andalusian committed $170 million to direct lending deals in the third quarter, and ZCG named a global head of capital formation. These show fundraising and hiring continuing, even as managers warn about the weaker end of the market. WSJ reports big investors are cutting their losses on troubled properties, a reminder that real-estate distress is still being worked out. Stress shows up on the household side too: home equity lines of credit are being used to pay down cards and buy cars, and federal loan caps are pushing graduate students toward private lenders. The NYT says developing-country debt has reached $9.4 trillion as high rates batter their economies.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's IPO is the day's event. The FT says it is set to price Wednesday. Reuters says Wall Street is preparing for a frenzy despite the broader AI stock slump. Crypto-futures markets point to a big first-day pop: Hyperliquid traders were pricing a 24% jump, per Yahoo Finance, and Bloomberg also flags strong AI-bull demand. New Street Research initiated at buy with a $105 target. Skeptics are loud: Seeking Alpha says the IPO 'does not compute', and one outlet pairs the record-scale pricing with safety warnings against a $1.4 trillion ambition. The Washington Post frames it as coming after a year when AI hype turned to fear. These pre-IPO trading signals are informal and should be treated cautiously.

Democrats won the Alaska Senate seat, taking their tally to 56 seats, which would shape the regulatory outlook. Defense-related dealmaking is building in Europe: the FT sees logic in an Iceye and Avio pairing as the first European defense-space merger. GM wants to double its defense revenue. Helsing is scaling back its Plymouth factory after losing a British navy contract, which shows how slow procurement can bite start-ups. In energy, EnQuest is selling its UK North Sea fields to Neo Next+ to focus on Asia. Medtronic's Contego purchase and Vertex's Genomics pact are covered in healthcare.
